claim: Replication origins are licensed by loading two Mcm2-7 helicases around DNA in a head-to-head conformation poised to initiate bidirectional replication.
source: Replication origins are licensed by loading two Mcm2-7 helicases around DNA in a head-to-head conformation poised to initiate bidirectional replication.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies (Abid Ali et al., 2017; Evrin et al., 2009; Li et al., 2015; Remus et al., 2009) that characterize the head-to-head helicase conformation.

claim: Helicase loading requires origin–recognition complex (ORC), Cdc6, and Cdt1.
source: This process requires origin–recognition complex (ORC), Cdc6, and Cdt1.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of DNA replication, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: A single ORC molecule recruits both Mcm2-7/Cdt1 complexes via similar interactions that end upon Cdt1 release in the large majority of helicase loading events.
source: In the large majority of events, we observed a single ORC molecule recruiting both Mcm2-7/Cdt1 complexes via similar interactions that end upon Cdt1 release.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-molecule FRET experiments described in the manuscript, particularly the data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Between first- and second-helicase recruitment, a rapid change in interactions between ORC and the first Mcm2-7 occurs.
source: Between first- and second-helicase recruitment, a rapid change in interactions between ORC and the first Mcm2-7 occurs.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of distinct FRET states (OM and MO interactions) in the single-molecule experiments.

claim: ORC breaks the interactions mediating first Mcm2-7 recruitment within seconds after first Cdt1 release.
source: Within seconds, ORC breaks the interactions mediating first Mcm2-7 recruitment, releases from its initial DNA-binding site, and forms a new interaction with the opposite face of the first Mcm2-7.
evidence: This is supported by the kinetic data showing the timing of OM interaction loss and MO interaction formation (Figures 4 and 6).

claim: ORC releases from its initial DNA-binding site after breaking first Mcm2-7 recruitment interactions.
source: Within seconds, ORC breaks the interactions mediating first Mcm2-7 recruitment, releases from its initial DNA-binding site, and forms a new interaction with the opposite face of the first Mcm2-7.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ORC is not bound to the primary ORC-binding site in the MO complex structure (Miller et al., 2019) and from the single-molecule data.

claim: ORC forms a new interaction with the opposite face of the first Mcm2-7 after releasing from its initial DNA-binding site.
source: Within seconds, ORC breaks the interactions mediating first Mcm2-7 recruitment, releases from its initial DNA-binding site, and forms a new interaction with the opposite face of the first Mcm2-7.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of MO-FRET in the single-molecule experiments (Figure 5).

claim: The rearrangement of ORC requires release of the first Cdt1.
source: This rearrangement requires release of the first Cdt1 and tethers ORC as it flips over the first Mcm2-7 to form an inverted Mcm2-7–ORC–DNA complex required for second-helicase recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that preventing Cdt1 release (using the Mcm2-75RA mutant) prevents MO complex formation (Figure 6).

claim: ORC flips over the first Mcm2-7 while tethered to it to form an inverted Mcm2-7–ORC–DNA complex.
source: This rearrangement requires release of the first Cdt1 and tethers ORC as it flips over the first Mcm2-7 to form an inverted Mcm2-7–ORC–DNA complex required for second-helicase recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of the MO complex and the mixed-labeling experiments showing that the same ORC interacts with both helicases (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: The inverted Mcm2-7–ORC–DNA complex is required for second-helicase recruitment.
source: This rearrangement requires release of the first Cdt1 and tethers ORC as it flips over the first Mcm2-7 to form an inverted Mcm2-7–ORC–DNA complex required for second-helicase recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that disrupting the MO complex (using ORC6∆N119 mutant) prevents second Mcm2-7 recruitment (Figure 5).

claim: The inverted Mcm2-7–ORC–DNA complex is maintained until head-to-head interactions between the two helicases are formed.
source: To ensure correct licensing, this complex is maintained until head-to-head interactions between the two helicases are formed.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that MO-FRET ends shortly after second Mcm2-7 arrival, coinciding with the timing of double-hexamer formation (Figure 6d).

claim: The Mcm2-7 complex is the core enzyme of the eukaryotic replicative helicase.
source: The Mcm2-7 complex is the core enzyme of the eukaryotic replicative helicase and its loading onto DNA is restricted to G1 phase (Aparicio et al., 1997; Diffley et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Mcm2-7 loading onto DNA is restricted to G1 phase.
source: The Mcm2-7 complex is the core enzyme of the eukaryotic replicative helicase and its loading onto DNA is restricted to G1 phase (Aparicio et al., 1997; Diffley et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Restricting helicase loading to G1 phase prevents helicases from being loaded onto replicated DNA, ensuring that no part of the genome is replicated more than once per cell cycle.
source: This constraint prevents helicases from being loaded onto replicated DNA, ensuring that no part of the genome is replicated more than once per cell cycle (Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: ORC binds origin DNA.
source: The origin–recognition complex (ORC) binds origin DNA and then recruits Cdc6 (Bell and Stillman, 1992; Speck et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: ORC recruits Cdc6 after binding origin DNA.
source: The origin–recognition complex (ORC) binds origin DNA and then recruits Cdc6 (Bell and Stillman, 1992; Speck et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The ORC–Cdc6 complex encircles the origin DNA.
source: The resulting ORC–Cdc6 complex encircles the origin DNA (Feng et al., 2021; Schmidt and Bleichert, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited.

claim: Mcm2-7 in complex with Cdt1 associates with ORC-Cdc6 and adjacent DNA to form the short-lived ORC–Cdc6–Cdt1–Mcm2-7 (OCCM) complex.
source: Mcm2-7 in complex with Cdt1 associates with ORC-Cdc6 and adjacent DNA to form the short-lived ORC–Cdc6–Cdt1–Mcm2-7 (OCCM) complex (Sun et al., 2013; Ticau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by structural and single-molecule studies cited.

claim: Loading of a second Cdt1-bound-Mcm2-7 hexamer, oriented in the opposite direction of the first, completes formation of the Mcm2-7 'double hexamer'.
source: Loading of a second Cdt1-bound-Mcm2-7 hexamer, oriented in the opposite direction of the first, completes formation of the Mcm2-7 'double hexamer'.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Natural origins include at least one additional weaker, inverted ORC-binding site in addition to a primary ORC-binding site.
source: In addition to a primary ORC-binding site, natural origins include at least one additional weaker, inverted ORC-binding site (Chang et al., 2011; Palzkill and Newlon, 1988; Wilmes and Bell, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by studies of origin architecture cited.

claim: The primary and secondary ORC-binding sites at natural origins are typically less than ~60 bp apart.
source: These sequences can be located at a variety of distances from one another but are typically less than ~60 bp apart (Chang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a study of origin architecture cited.

claim: Mutations in the Mcm3 C-terminus predicted to interfere with interactions between Mcm2-7 and the ORC–Cdc6 complex prevent recruitment of both the first and second helicases.
source: This model is supported by evidence that mutations in the Mcm3 C-terminus predicted to interfere with interactions between Mcm2-7 and the ORC–Cdc6 complex prevent recruitment of both the first and second helicases (Coster and Diffley, 2017; Frigola et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by mutational studies cited.

claim: Two ORC DNA-binding sites are required for successful helicase loading in vitro and origin function in vivo in ensemble experiments.
source: In addition, for ensemble experiments two ORC DNA-binding sites are required for successful helicase loading in vitro and origin function in vivo (Coster and Diffley, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by an ensemble study cited.

claim: Single-molecule helicase-loading experiments with the ARS1 origin showed that a single ORC molecule can direct loading of both Mcm2-7 helicases.
source: In contrast, single-molecule helicase-loading experiments with the ARS1 origin showed that a single ORC molecule can direct loading of both Mcm2-7 helicases (Ticau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a single-molecule study cited.

claim: Time-resolved cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM) experiments show predominantly one ORC molecule bound to the DNA in each helicase-loading intermediate observed on the ARS1 origin.
source: A single ORC model is also supported by time-resolved cryoelectron microscopy (cryo-EM) experiments showing predominantly one ORC molecule bound to the DNA in each helicase-loading intermediate observed on the ARS1 origin (Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cryo-EM study cited.

claim: ORC bends DNA prior to Mcm2-7 recruitment.
source: ORC has been shown to bend DNA prior to Mcm2-7 recruitment (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a structural study cited.

claim: Cryo-EM studies of the OCCM intermediate show that the first Mcm2-7 hexamer interacts with and encircles the DNA adjacent to ORC–Cdc6.
source: Cryo-EM studies of the OCCM intermediate show that the first Mcm2-7 hexamer interacts with and encircles the DNA adjacent to ORC–Cdc6 (Sun et al., 2013; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM studies cited.

claim: Interaction of the C-terminal region of ORC with the C-terminal region of Mcm2-7 mediates recruitment of the first Mcm2-7 hexamer.
source: These and related structures also reveal that interaction of the C-terminal region of ORC with the C-terminal region of Mcm2-7 mediates recruitment of the first Mcm2-7 hexamer (Yuan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required to proceed beyond the OCCM.
source: ATP hydrolysis is required to proceed beyond the OCCM, and structures of intermediates on-pathway to the Mcm2-7 double hexamer had been elusive until a recent time-resolved cryo-EM study (Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: A time-resolved cryo-EM study observed a complex in which an inverted ORC is engaged with the N-terminal region of the first Mcm2-7.
source: Intriguingly, this study observed a complex in which an inverted ORC is engaged with the N-terminal region of the first Mcm2-7.
evidence: This is supported by a cryo-EM study cited (Miller et al., 2019).

claim: Single-molecule studies demonstrated that the two Mcm2-7 complexes in each double-hexamer associate with origin DNA in a one-at-a-time manner.
source: Single-molecule studies demonstrated that the two Mcm2-7 complexes in each double-hexamer associate with origin DNA in a one-at-a-time manner (Ticau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a single-molecule study cited.

claim: Single-molecule FRET (sm-FRET) has been used to monitor opening and closing of the interface between Mcm2 and Mcm5.
source: Single-molecule FRET (sm-FRET) has been used to monitor opening and closing of the interface between Mcm2 and Mcm5 (Bochman and Schwacha, 2008; Samel et al., 2014) that provides DNA access to the central channel of the Mcm2-7 ring (Ticau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule FRET studies cited.

claim: Mcm2-7 is recruited with an open gate that closes around origin DNA substantially after initial DNA association.
source: These studies revealed that Mcm2-7 is recruited with an open gate that closes around origin DNA substantially after initial DNA association.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule FRET studies cited (Ticau et al., 2017).

claim: Recruitment and loading of each Mcm2-7 involves a separate set of Cdc6 and Cdt1 molecules.
source: Such approaches also revealed that recruitment and loading of each Mcm2-7 involves a separate set of Cdc6 and Cdt1 molecules.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule studies cited (Ticau et al., 2015; Ticau et al., 2017).

claim: Following each Mcm2-7 recruitment, Cdc6 and Cdt1 are released sequentially.
source: Following each Mcm2-7 recruitment, Cdc6 and Cdt1 are released sequentially, and the Mcm2-7 ring closes concomitant with Cdt1 release (Ticau et al., 2015; Ticau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule studies cited.

claim: The Mcm2-7 ring closes concomitant with Cdt1 release.
source: Following each Mcm2-7 recruitment, Cdc6 and Cdt1 are released sequentially, and the Mcm2-7 ring closes concomitant with Cdt1 release (Ticau et al., 2015; Ticau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule studies cited.

claim: Structural data suggest that Cdt1 holds the Mcm2-7 ring open at the Mcm2-5 gate.
source: This connection between Cdt1 release and ring closing is consistent with structural data that suggest that Cdt1 holds the Mcm2-7 ring open at the Mcm2-5 gate (Frigola et al., 2017; Zhai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited.

claim: Fluorescent labels on ORC5C-549 and Mcm2-72C-649 did not interfere with protein function in ensemble helicase-loading assays.
source: Importantly, the fluorescent labels did not interfere with protein function in ensemble helicase-loading assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the ensemble helicase-loading assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the majority of double-hexamer formation events (81%), one ORC molecule loaded two Mcm2-7 complexes.
source: Specifically, we observed association of one ORC molecule with the DNA throughout the interval for sequential recruitment of two Mcm2-7 molecules in 81% of double-hexamer formation events.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule colocalization data.

claim: 88 ± 2% of the ORC5C-549 protein was labeled.
source: The observation of only one ORC is not due to incomplete ORC labeling as we determined that 88 ± 2% of the ORC5C-549 protein was labeled (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the labeling efficiency measurement described in Materials and methods.

claim: Two ORC proteins were observed during sequential Mcm2-7 recruitment in only 13% of the double-hexamer formation events.
source: In contrast, we observed two ORC proteins during sequential Mcm2-7 recruitment in only 13% of the double-hexamer formation events (22/166).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule colocalization data.

claim: In 8/166 double-hexamer formation events, different ORC molecules were present during the two Mcm2-7 associations.
source: In 8/166 events, different ORC molecules were present during the two Mcm2-7 associations.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule colocalization data.

claim: The rare events with different ORC molecules present during the two Mcm2-7 associations provide the first direct evidence of helicase loading mediated by two separate ORC molecules.
source: These rare events provide the first direct evidence of helicase loading mediated by two separate ORC molecules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of two-ORC events in the single-molecule data.

claim: High EFRET values between ORC5C-549 and Mcm2-72C-649 arise from interactions between ORC and Mcm2-7.
source: Three findings give us confidence that these high EFRET values arise from interactions between ORC and Mcm2-7.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence: (1) fluorophores positioned based on OCCM structure, (2) high EFRET detected simultaneously with Mcm2-7 arrival, (3) dependence on fluorophore placement.

claim: In 105/111 instances where a first Mcm2-72C-650 arrived at an ORC5C-549-bound DNA, high EFRET was detected at the same time as the arrival of the Mcm2-7 on DNA (temporal resolution is ±2.4 s).
source: Second, in 105/111 instances where a first Mcm2-72C-650 arrived at an ORC5C-549-bound DNA, high EFRET was detected at the same time as the arrival of the Mcm2-7 on DNA (temporal resolution is ±2.4 s; Figure 1—figure supplement 2b, c).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b, c.

claim: Moving the label on either ORC or Mcm2-7 to the opposite side of the protein relative to the C-terminal ORC–Mcm2-7 interface seen in the OCCM resulted in strong reductions in the associated EFRET values.
source: Finally, we verified that observing high EFRET was dependent on the placement of the fluorescent probes on Mcm2-7 and ORC. Moving the label on either ORC or Mcm2-7 to the opposite side of the protein relative to the C-terminal ORC–Mcm2-7 interface seen in the OCCM resulted in strong reductions in the associated EFRET values (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data with alternative labeling positions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total emission upon donor excitation is enhanced during OM interactions due to protein-induced fluorescence enhancement (PIFE) of the DY549P1 fluorophore.
source: We note that the total emission upon donor excitation is enhanced during OM interactions (Figure 1c, black: Dex, (Dem + Aem) panel). This is due to protein-induced fluorescence enhancement (Hwang et al., 2011) of the of the DY549P1 fluorophore during the OM interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the observation of enhanced total emission during OM-FRET and the control experiments with Cy3B and ORC6C-549 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Arrival of each of the two Mcm2-7 helicases was accompanied by a short period of high EFRET in almost all cases (106/111 double-hexamer formation events).
source: Arrival of each of the two Mcm2-7 helicases was accompanied by a short period of high EFRET in almost all cases (Figure 1c, blue: Dex, [Aem/(Aem+Dem)] panel). In 111 examples of double-hexamer formation, 106 showed distinct periods of high EFRET with each of the two Mcm2-7 arrivals (see below for a description of the remaining 5/111 cases).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data shown in Figure 1c and the analysis of 111 double-hexamer formation events.

claim: The start time of the first OM interaction matched the first Mcm2-7 arrival in 104/106 cases.
source: The start time of the first OM interaction matched the first Mcm2-7 arrival in 104/106 cases and the start of the second OM interaction matched the arrival of the second Mcm2-7 in 98/106 cases (time resolution of experiment ~ 2.4 s).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data.

claim: The start of the second OM interaction matched the arrival of the second Mcm2-7 in 98/106 cases.
source: The start time of the first OM interaction matched the first Mcm2-7 arrival in 104/106 cases and the start of the second OM interaction matched the arrival of the second Mcm2-7 in 98/106 cases (time resolution of experiment ~ 2.4 s).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data.

claim: The similar mean EFRET values associated with the first and second OM interactions (0.72 ± 0.01 and 0.79 ± 0.01, respectively) indicate that recruitment of the first and second Mcm2-7 is mediated by the formation of a similar ORC–Mcm2-7 interface.
source: The similar mean EFRET values associated with the first and second OM interactions (0.72 ± 0.01 and 0.79 ± 0.01, respectively; Figure 1d) indicate that recruitment of the first and second Mcm2-7 is mediated by the formation of a similar ORC–Mcm2-7 interface.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of the EFRET values shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The first OM interaction consistently ended before the second Mcm2-7 was recruited during helicase loading (106/106 cases).
source: The first OM interaction consistently ended before the second Mcm2-7 was recruited during helicase loading. Although both ORC and first Mcm2-7 remained associated with the DNA, the OM-FRET signal was lost before second Mcm2-7 arrival in 106/106 cases.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data.

claim: EFRET values in the 10-s interval preceding the second Mcm2-7 arrival were low, with an average value of 0.08 ± 0.02.
source: Consistent with this observation, EFRET values in the 10-s interval preceding the second Mcm2-7 arrival were low (Figure 1d, middle panel), with an average value of 0.08 ± 0.02.
evidence: This is supported by the EFRET histogram shown in Figure 1d, middle panel.

claim: The second OM interaction ended with the loss of ORC5C-549 fluorescence in 71/106 events.
source: The second OM interaction observed was also short lived and in a majority of events ended with the loss of ORC5C-549 fluorescence (71/106; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: The loss of donor fluorescence at the end of the second OM interaction was typically not due to photobleaching.
source: We confirmed this loss of donor fluorescence was typically not due to photobleaching (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b), indicating that the end of the second OM interaction in these cases was concomitant with the departure of ORC from the DNA.
evidence: This is supported by the photobleaching rate measurement shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4b.

claim: The observation of two sequential OM interactions with a single ORC protein could arise from ORC5C-549 interacting twice with the first Mcm2-72C-649 (Re-FRET model).
source: The two high EFRET signals could arise due to ORC5C-549 interacting twice with the first Mcm2-72C-649 (Figure 2a, Model 1, 'Re-FRET').
evidence: This is a hypothetical model proposed to explain the data.

claim: The observation of two sequential OM interactions with a single ORC protein could arise from ORC5C-549 interacting with each of the two Mcm2-72C-649 complexes on arrival at the DNA (ORC-flip model).
source: Alternatively, ORC5C-549 may instead interact with each of the two Mcm2-72C-649 complexes on arrival at the DNA (Model 2).
evidence: This is a hypothetical model proposed to explain the data.

claim: To achieve the head-to-head conformation of the Mcm2-7 helicases in the double hexamer under the ORC-flip model, either ORC or the first Mcm2-7 must invert its orientation on the DNA.
source: To achieve the head-to-head conformation of the Mcm2-7 helicases in the double hexamer, Model 2 would require either ORC or the first Mcm2-7 to invert its orientation on the DNA.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the geometry of the double hexamer.

claim: Previous studies found no evidence of Mcm2-5 gate reopening during helicase loading.
source: Since initial loading of the Mcm2-7 complex involves passing origin DNA through the Mcm2-5 gate followed by gate closing, inversion of Mcm2-7 on the DNA would require reopening of the Mcm2-5 gate. However, previous studies found no evidence of Mcm2-5 gate reopening during helicase loading (Ticau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a previous single-molecule study cited.

claim: The version of the ORC-flip model in which ORC rebinds the DNA on the opposite side of the first Mcm2-7 and in the opposite orientation is most likely.
source: For this reason, the version of Model 2 in which ORC rebinds the DNA on the opposite side of the first Mcm2-7 and in the opposite orientation is most likely. We call this the 'ORC-flip' model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of evidence for Mcm2-5 gate reopening.

claim: In the experiment with mixed Mcm2-72C-649 and Mcm2-74N-650, four distinct patterns of OM interaction profiles were observed at similar frequencies.
source: We observed four distinct patterns of OM interaction profiles at similar frequencies when the differently labeled Mcm2-7 complexes were present (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Of 90 double-hexamer formation events with mixed Mcm2-72C-649 and Mcm2-74N-650, 25 events had 2 OM-FRET peaks and 21 events had no associated OM-FRET.
source: Of 90 double-hexamer formation events, we identified 25 events with 2 OM-FRET peaks and 21 events with no associated OM-FRET.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data.

claim: Approximately half the double-hexamer formation events with mixed Mcm2-72C-649 and Mcm2-74N-650 had a single OM-FRET peak associated with them (44/90).
source: Strikingly, approximately half the double-hexamer formation events had a single OM-FRET peak associated with them (44/90), consistent with the ORC-flip model (see Figure 2b, CN and NC panels).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data.

claim: The single OM-FRET events with mixed Mcm2-72C-649 and Mcm2-74N-650 are equally distributed between events in which FRET is associated with the first (22/90 events) or the second (22/90 events) Mcm2-7 arrival.
source: Also consistent with this model, these single OM-FRET events are equally distributed between events in which FRET is associated with the first (22/90 events) or the second (22/90 events) Mcm2-7 arrival (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Both the presence of the four patterns of FRET and their equal frequency strongly support the ORC-flip model.
source: Indeed, based on the EFRET patterns, we were able to infer the underlying double-hexamer 'type' for each OM-FRET pattern revealing similar frequencies of CC, NN, CN, and NC double hexamers. Both the presence of the four patterns of FRET and their equal frequency strongly support the ORC-flip model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the mixed-labeling experiment.

claim: In the experiment with only C-terminally labeled Mcm2-7 (Figure 1), 1/111 events showed FRET only with the first Mcm2-7 arrival and 3/111 events showed FRET only with the second Mcm2-7 arrival.
source: We observed 1/111 events in which only the first Mcm2-7 arrival exhibited FRET and 3/111 events in which only the second Mcm2-7 arrival exhibited FRET.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data.

claim: In the experiment with only C-terminally labeled Mcm2-7 (Figure 1), 1/111 events showed no FRET on either Mcm2-7 arrival.
source: We also observed 1/111 events with no FRET on either Mcm2-7 arrival.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data.

claim: The rare events with one or no FRET peaks in the experiment with only C-terminally labeled Mcm2-7 are likely to arise from DNAs with two bound ORC molecules, one of which is unlabeled.
source: Although all five events appear to have a single ORC colocalized with DNA, these events are likely to arise from DNAs with two bound ORC molecules, one of which is unlabeled.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low frequency of these events and the labeling efficiency.

claim: ORC makes OM interactions with both the first and second Mcm2-7 helicases during helicase loading.
source: Thus, we conclude that ORC makes OM interactions with both the first and second Mcm2-7 helicases during helicase loading.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mixed-labeling experiments.

claim: In the experiment with mixed ORC5C-549 and ORC1N-550, of 82 double-hexamer formation events, 37 events had two OM-FRET peaks (fraction of events is 0.45 ± 0.05) and 41 events had no associated OM-FRET (0.50 ± 0.06).
source: Of 82 double-hexamer formation events, 37 events had two OM-FRET peaks (fraction of events is 0.45 ± 0.05; Figure 3d) and 41 events had no associated OM-FRET (0.50 ± 0.06).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In the experiment with mixed ORC5C-549 and ORC1N-550, 1/82 events were consistent with a CN ORC pair (0.01 ± 0.01) and 3/82 events with NC ORC pairs (0.04 ± 0.02).
source: We identified 1/82 events that was consistent with a CN ORC pair (0.01 ± 0.01) and 3/82 events with NC ORC pairs (0.04 ± 0.02).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule FRET data.

claim: The vast majority of events in the mixed ORC experiment are of CC and NN types (78/82), which is consistent with the same ORC interacting with both Mcm2-7 helicases.
source: However, the vast majority of events are of CC and NN types (78/82), which is consistent with the same ORC interacting with both Mcm2-7 helicases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the mixed-ORC-labeling experiment.

claim: The rare CN and NC events in the mixed ORC experiment are most likely two ORC events in which one ORC is unlabeled.
source: The rare CN and NC events are most likely two ORC events in which one ORC is unlabeled (see above).
evidence: This is an inference based on the low frequency of these events and the labeling efficiency.

claim: The majority of helicase loading events involve one ORC molecule interacting sequentially with both helicases (one-ORC model).
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that the majority of events involve one ORC molecule interacting sequentially with both helicases (one-ORC model).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mixed-ORC-labeling experiment.

claim: In a subset of events with more than one fluorescent ORC present during loading (7/27), the first ORC disappeared before the second one arrived, suggesting a two-ORC mechanism.
source: In a subset of these events (7/27) the first ORC disappeared before the second one arrived, suggesting a two-ORC mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule colocalization data.

claim: In 20/27 events with more than one fluorescent ORC, a second ORC associated between the first and second Mcm2-7 recruitment events while the first ORC remained present throughout.
source: We also observed 20/27 events in which a second ORC associated between the first and second Mcm2-7 recruitment events while the first ORC remained present throughout.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule colocalization data.

source: ORC binding to origin DNA is stimulated by ATP but not ADP (Bell and Stillman, 1992), suggesting ORC ATP hydrolysis could facilitate release of ORC from its initial binding site.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: Cdc6 completes the ORC–Cdc6 protein ring around the DNA.
source: Cdc6 completes the ORC–Cdc6 protein ring around the DNA (Yuan et al., 2017) and Cdc6 ATP hydrolysis is required to release Cdc6 (Coster et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2014), suggesting that this hydrolysis event also is required for ORC DNA release.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical studies cited.

claim: Cdc6 ATP hydrolysis is required to release Cdc6.
source: Cdc6 completes the ORC–Cdc6 protein ring around the DNA (Yuan et al., 2017) and Cdc6 ATP hydrolysis is required to release Cdc6 (Coster et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2014), suggesting that this hydrolysis event also is required for ORC DNA release.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical studies cited.

claim: A model in which the MO complex is required to recruit the second Mcm2-7 is consistent with origin architecture in budding yeast, wherein two ORC-binding sites with different affinities are required for helicase-loading in vivo.
source: A model in which the MO complex is required to recruit the second Mcm2-7 is consistent with origin architecture in budding yeast, wherein two ORC-binding sites with different affinities are required for helicase-loading in vivo.
evidence: This is a comparison to known origin architecture.

claim: Natural origins have selected against an architecture with two oppositely oriented strong ORC-binding sites.
source: Interestingly, even though two oppositely oriented strong ORC-binding sites support origin function both in vitro and in vivo (Coster and Diffley, 2017), natural origins have selected against this architecture (Chang et al., 2011; Marahrens and Stillman, 1992; Palzkill and Newlon, 1988; Rao et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by studies of origin architecture cited.

claim: When B2 elements have been mapped they are frequently located at positions in which the presence of the OCCM (OC6C1M1 in Figure 7) would clash with ORC binding at B2.
source: Indeed, when B2 elements have been mapped they are frequently located at positions in which the presence of the OCCM (OC6C1M1 in Figure 7) would clash with ORC binding at B2 (Chang et al., 2011; Marahrens and Stillman, 1992; Rao et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by studies of origin architecture cited.

claim: In the small number of two ORC events observed, second ORC associations occur after the first, but before the second, Mcm2-7 arrives.
source: Along these lines, in the small number of two ORC events in our studies, we observe second ORC associations occur after the first, but before the second, Mcm2-7 arrives.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule colocalization data.

claim: Whether one or two ORCs mediate loading, the ORC mediating second Mcm2-7 recruitment would only stably associate with B2 after the first Mcm2-7 is recruited.
source: Thus, we propose that, whether one or two ORCs mediate loading, the ORC mediating second Mcm2-7 recruitment would only stably associate with B2 after the first Mcm2-7 is recruited.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the experimental data and origin architecture.

claim: The pre-M1O slides in search of a second, inverted ORC-binding site and recruits the second Mcm2-7 only once an inverted ORC-binding site is found.
source: We speculate that the pre-M1O slides in search of a second, inverted ORC-binding site (Figure 7) and recruits the second Mcm2-7 only once an inverted ORC-binding site is found.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proposed model and origin architecture.

claim: A number of helicase-loading intermediates slide in vitro.
source: A number of helicase-loading intermediates slide in vitro (Sánchez et al., 2021; Scherr et al., 2021), and experiments placing barriers to sliding at ARS1 support a role for sliding to identify second inverted ORC-binding sites (Coster and Diffley, 2017; Warner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by studies cited.

claim: Helicase loading does not occur at artificial origins with a single strong ORC-binding site.
source: Consistent with the argument that second Mcm2-7 recruitment only occurs when the sliding pre-M1O finds a second inverted ORC-binding site, helicase loading does not occur at artificial origins with a single strong ORC-binding site (Coster and Diffley, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a study cited.

claim: Analyses of helicase loading with the ORC6∆N119 mutant and first Mcm2-7 helicases that fail to form the MO interaction show that in both cases the Mcm2-7 molecules are rapidly released from the DNA after ORC release.
source: Analyses of helicase loading with the ORC6∆N119 mutant and first Mcm2-7 helicases that fail to form the MO interaction show that in both cases the Mcm2-7 molecules are rapidly released from the DNA after ORC release (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The finding that the first Mcm2-7 is unstable if the MO complex is not formed indicates that there would be only a short-time window for a second ORC molecule to form an MO complex before the first Mcm2-7 is released.
source: This finding indicates that the first Mcm2-7 is unstable if the MO complex is not formed and that there would be only a short-time window for a second ORC molecule to form an MO complex before the first Mcm2-7 is released.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Mcm2-7 dwell time data.

claim: The low frequency of two-ORC events observed suggests that the first ORC has a higher probability of forming the MO complex through a helicase-tethered flip than a second ORC.
source: The low frequency of two-ORC events we observe (see Figure 3) suggests that the first ORC has a higher probability of forming the MO complex through a helicase-tethered flip than a second ORC, consistent with the first ORC already being associated with the first Mcm2-7.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency of two-ORC events.

claim: Higher ORC concentrations might increase the frequency of two-ORC events.
source: Given the short-time window for a second ORC to act, higher ORC concentrations might increase the frequency of two-ORC events.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the kinetic considerations.

claim: In vivo footprinting studies show that only a subset of the origin-associated stronger ACS-binding sites are occupied by ORC in cells.
source: Nevertheless, consistent with ORC being limiting in cells, in vivo footprinting studies show that only a subset of the origin-associated stronger ACS-binding sites are occupied by ORC in cells (Belsky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by an in vivo footprinting study cited.

claim: The much weaker B2-binding sites are unlikely to stably bind ORC without additional interactions.
source: This finding suggests that the much weaker B2-binding sites are unlikely to stably bind ORC without additional interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vivo footprinting data.

claim: If a second ORC is involved in vivo it would only be recruited after the first Mcm2-7 is origin associated.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that if a second ORC is involved in vivo it would only be recruited after the first Mcm2-7 is origin associated.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the in vivo footprinting data and the proposed model.

claim: Release of the first Cdt1 is a critical regulatory step in helicase loading.
source: Our data show that release of the first Cdt1 is a critical regulatory step in helicase loading.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic data on Cdt1 release and OM/MO interactions.

claim: Cdt1 binding could be required for OM interactions such that Cdt1 release reduces or eliminates these interactions.
source: Cdt1 binding could be required for OM interactions such that Cdt1 release reduces or eliminates these interactions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of OM interaction loss.

claim: Cdt1 binding has been proposed to alleviate an autoinhibitory function of Mcm2-7, thereby allowing interaction with ORC-CdcDNA.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, Cdt1 binding has been proposed to alleviate an autoinhibitory function of Mcm2-7, thereby allowing interaction with ORC-CdcDNA (Fernández-Cid et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a study cited.

claim: Closure of the Mcm2-5 gate, which is concomitant with Cdt1 release, may induce a conformational change in the Mcm2-7 complex that disrupts the OM interaction.
source: A second possibility is that closure of the Mcm2-5 gate, which is concomitant with Cdt1 release (Ticau et al., 2017), induces a conformational change in the Mcm2-7 complex that disrupts the OM interaction.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of OM interaction loss.

claim: ORC is frequently released from the DNA simultaneously with the second Cdt1 release.
source: It is intriguing to note that ORC is frequently released from the DNA simultaneously with the second Cdt1 release (Ticau et al., 2015), suggesting that in addition to breaking the OM interaction, release of the first Cdt1 may stimulate ORC release from DNA.
evidence: This is supported by a previous single-molecule study cited.

claim: Release of the first Cdt1 and the concomitant closure of the Mcm2-5 gate around DNA likely create a new interaction site on Mcm2-7 for Orc6.
source: Release of the first Cdt1 and the concomitant closure of the Mcm2-5 gate around DNA likely create a new interaction site on Mcm2-7 for Orc6 (Miller et al., 2019; Ticau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural and single-molecule data cited.

claim: The N- and C-terminal domains of Orc6 (Orc6N and Orc6C) interact with Cdt1 in vitro.
source: The N- and C-terminal domains of Orc6 (Orc6N and Orc6C) interact with Cdt1 in vitro (Chen and Bell, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a biochemical study cited.

claim: Once the first Cdt1 is released, Orc6N is able to reach over the first Mcm2-7 and establish a tether with the Mcm2 N-terminal region.
source: We propose that once the first Cdt1 is released, Orc6N is able to reach over the first Mcm2-7 and establish a tether with the Mcm2 N-terminal region (Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a proposal based on structural data cited.

claim: The extensive linker (~160 amino acids) between the Orc6N and Orc6C serves as flexible leash that facilitates a search for the new Orc6N-binding site.
source: In this model, the extensive linker (~160 amino acids) between the Orc6N and Orc6C serves as flexible leash that facilitates a search for this new Orc6N-binding site (Chen and Bell, 2011).
evidence: This is a proposal based on the structure of Orc6.

claim: Since ORC is not Cdc6 bound at the OM1 stage, ORC forms an open ring around DNA and can release from its primary DNA-binding site.
source: Since ORC is not Cdc6 bound at this stage (OM1 state), ORC forms an open ring around DNA and can release from its primary DNA-binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed model and knowledge of ORC structure.

claim: The closed Mcm2-5 gate in the M1O facilitates contacts between Orc6C and the Mcm5 N-terminal region such that the two domains of Orc6 form a latch across the Mcm2-5 gate.
source: The closed Mcm2-5 gate in the M1O facilitates contacts between Orc6C and the Mcm5 N-terminal region such that the two domains of Orc6 form a latch across the Mcm2-5 gate (Miller et al., 2019), a likely mechanism for the MO complex stabilizing DNA association of the first Mcm2-7 after loss of the OM interaction (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a proposal based on structural data cited and the Mcm2-7 dwell time data.

claim: Orc6N is required to form the MO interaction.
source: We show that Orc6N is required to form the MO interaction, and that release of the first Cdt1 and formation of the MO interaction occur in close succession.
evidence: This is supported by the experiments with the ORC6∆N119 mutant.

claim: A single-ORC mechanism for helicase loading has potential implications for DNA replication initiation in higher eukaryotes.
source: A single-ORC mechanism for helicase loading has potential implications for DNA replication initiation in higher eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: ORC does not exhibit sequence-specific binding in higher eukaryotes where origins are not defined by specific DNA sequences.
source: Although the helicase-loading proteins from budding yeast are highly conserved, ORC does not exhibit sequence-specific binding in higher eukaryotes where origins are not defined by specific DNA sequences (Bleichert et al., 2017; Prioleau and MacAlpine, 2016; Vashee et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: A mechanism in which two separate ORC molecules guide loading of the two helicases would require two independent nonspecific ORC-binding events.
source: A mechanism in which two separate ORC molecules guide loading of the two helicases would require two independent nonspecific ORC-binding events.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements of a two-ORC mechanism in higher eukaryotes.

claim: In a two-ORC mechanism, each single Mcm2-7 helicase would then have to find an oppositely oriented helicase to complete helicase loading.
source: Each single Mcm2-7 helicase would then have to find an oppositely oriented helicase to complete helicase loading.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements of a two-ORC mechanism in higher eukaryotes.

claim: Helicase loading guided by a single ORC that performs an inversion places fewer constraints on where helicases can be loaded and could still be supported with low ORC concentrations.
source: In contrast, helicase loading guided by a single ORC that performs an inversion places fewer constraints on where helicases can be loaded and could still be supported with low ORC concentrations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the advantages of a single-ORC mechanism in higher eukaryotes.

claim: A full round of helicase loading completed by a single ORC could prevent non-productive loading of single helicases that cannot support bidirectional replication.
source: Additionally, a full round of helicase loading completed by a single ORC could prevent non-productive loading of single helicases that cannot support bidirectional replication (Champasa et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about the advantages of a single-ORC mechanism, supported by citations.
